extracted.intended_audience: educators, curriculum planners, teachers, and educational theorists
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for designing school curricula that connect subject-matter to social life through active occupations, play, and integrated study of geography and history. Emphasizes starting from learners' experience, using raw materials and purposeful activities to foster intellectual and social development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narrow utilitarian selection of subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: "Democracy cannot flourish where the chief influences in selecting subject matter of instruction are utilitarian ends narrowly conceived..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricula must not be chosen primarily to prepare masses for narrow utilitarian labor or to maintain class traditions. Reject treating the 'essentials' (e.g., the three R's) as mechanically sufficient; instead choose subject-matter that supports democratic ideals and meaningful, freely chosen activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present situations relevant to living together
rubrics_metrics.description: "A curriculum which acknowledges the social responsibilities of education must present situations where problems are relevant to the problems of living together..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design learning situations so observation and information develop social insight and interest. Subjects should connect with social responsibilities and cooperative living rather than abstract, isolated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat subject matter as meanings that supply social content
rubrics_metrics.description: "The subject matter of education consists primarily of the meanings which supply content to existing social life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select, formulate, and organize material so it transmits socially relevant meanings to the next generation. Avoid making subject-matter an end in itself detached from pupils' activities and social experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with active occupations of social origin and move to scientific insight
rubrics_metrics.description: "The young begin with active occupations having a social origin and use, and proceed to a scientific insight in the materials and laws involved..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start instruction from learners' practical, socially-rooted activities; use these as entry points for introducing ideas, facts, and scientific principles communicated by broader experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start from learners' experience and capacities; introduce play and work like out-of-school activities
rubrics_metrics.description: "The desirability of starting from and with the experience and capacities of learners... has led to the introduction of forms of activity, in play and work, similar to those in which children and youth engage outside of school."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design lessons that mirror children's outside activities to engage the whole pupil, reduce the school-life gap, make learning easier, and provide social contexts for cooperative information-sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value play and active work as intellectual and social, not mere diversions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The grounds for assigning to play and active work a definite place in the curriculum are intellectual and social, not matters of temporary expediency and momentary agreeableness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use play and constructive occupations for sustained educational ends—cognitive development, social disposition, and motivation—rather than as only relief from regular work or ephemeral amusements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate manual skill to intellectual results and socialized disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: "The problem of the educator is to engage pupils in these activities in such ways that while manual skill and technical efficiency are gained... these things shall be subordinated to education--that is, to intellectual results and the forming of a socialized disposition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using manual activities, ensure their primary purpose is cognitive growth and social development; technical proficiency should serve broader educational aims, not replace them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly prescribed, model-reproducing activities
rubrics_metrics.description: "Activities which follow definite prescription and dictation or which reproduce without modification ready-made models... do not require the perception and elaboration of ends..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject tasks that merely reproduce models or follow rigid prescriptions. Provide opportunities requiring judgment, selection of means, and allowance for mistakes so pupils exercise initiative and problem-solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide opportunities for making mistakes and learning limits
rubrics_metrics.description: "Opportunity for making mistakes is an incidental requirement... limitation of capacity is one of the things which has to be learned; like other things, it is learned through the experience of consequences."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities that allow safe mistakes and reveal limitations, using teacher guidance to timely expose inadequacies and stimulate improved, appropriately challenging efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor crude/raw materials over only perfected/formatted materials
rubrics_metrics.description: "Only by starting with crude material and subjecting it to purposeful handling will he gain the intelligence embodied in finished material."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply unrefined materials that require purposeful handling; avoid overreliance on pre-shaped or 'perfected' materials that prevent error, initiative, and authentic problem-solving—these lead to technical, not intelligent, learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus active occupations on wholes (purposes) rather than isolated elements
rubrics_metrics.description: "Active occupations should be concerned primarily with wholes... Wholes for purposes of education are not, however, physical affairs. Intellectually the existence of a whole depends upon a concern or interest..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame tasks around meaningful purposes that give elements a single meaning within a larger enterprise. Avoid isolating elements as 'simple' facts divorced from purposeful action and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use occupations that typify social situations (food, shelter, clothing, production, exchange)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Men's fundamental common concerns center about food, shelter, clothing, household furnishings, and the appliances connected with production, exchange, and consumption."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select occupations that reflect basic social concerns so they tap deep instincts and naturally integrate factual and principled knowledge with social relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach school occupations free from pecuniary motives; emphasize intrinsic value
rubrics_metrics.description: "In schools, occupations are not carried on for pecuniary gain but for their own content... Freed from extraneous associations... they supply modes of experience which are intrinsically valuable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure school work so its primary motive is intrinsic interest and learning, not monetary reward, thereby making occupational learning liberalizing and transferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use occupations as avenues into scientific and social study
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: gardening affords study of botany, soil chemistry, light, air; history and civics approached through industrial occupations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate subject-studies with practical occupations so content (science, social science) grows out of activity and becomes natural, correlated, and investigable rather than arbitary classroom facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active occupations introduce and exemplify the experimental method
rubrics_metrics.description: "The active occupations in which appliances are brought to bear upon physical things with the intention of effecting useful changes is the most vital introduction to the experimental method."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hands-on, goal-directed occupations to teach hypothesis-testing, control of conditions, observation of effects, and experimental thinking rather than abstract logic alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize play and work share purposeful features; difference is primarily time-span and continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Both involve ends consciously entertained and the selection and adaptations of materials and processes designed to effect the desired ends... The difference between them is largely one of time-span..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities understanding play and work are on a continuum; many educational activities can be both playful and purposeful. Emphasize continuity of ends and progressive complexity rather than strict separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent work from becoming drudgery by preserving intrinsic ends
rubrics_metrics.description: "Activity carried on under conditions of external pressure or coercion is... a mere means for avoiding some penalty, or for gaining some reward... Under unfree economic conditions... Work or industry offers little to engage the emotions and the imagination."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid coercive, externally-pressured tasks. Ensure the ends of activities are intrinsic to the action so work remains engaging and imaginative rather than mechanical drudgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the play-attitude in work to foster art and intrinsic motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Work which remains permeated with the play attitude is art--in quality if not in conventional designation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage freedom, creativity, and intrinsic interest in extended tasks so that sustained work retains qualities of play and aesthetic engagement, supporting lasting habits of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide for wholesome recreation and train capacity for recreative leisure
rubrics_metrics.description: "Education has no more serious responsibility than making adequate provision for enjoyment of recreative leisure... Art is again the answer to this demand."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include opportunities for healthy recreation and aesthetic experience that replenish energy and build lifelong capacities for meaningful leisure; neglect leads to unhealthy outlets (e.g., gambling, drink).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geography and history to extend meanings of primary activities
rubrics_metrics.description: "Geography and history supply subject matter which gives background and outlook, intellectual perspective, to what might otherwise be narrow personal actions or mere forms of technical skill."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach geography and history linked to students' activities so ordinary acts gain enduring substance, spatial and temporal perspective, and wider connections rather than remaining isolated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach geography/history integrated with life to avoid unassimilated information
rubrics_metrics.description: "If geography and history are taught as ready-made studies... it easily happens that a large number of statements about things remote and alien to everyday experience are learned... Mere amassing of information apart from the direct interests of life makes mind wooden."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid teaching geography and history as abstract, detached facts. Instead, integrate them into purposeful activity and direct interests so information is assimilated, animates experience, and preserves mental elasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply an environment that rewards curiosity and the reaching-out of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the business of educators to supply an environment so that this reaching out of an experience may be fruitfully rewarded and kept continuously active."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create learning environments where activities naturally lead learners to seek further information; structure opportunities that make connections perceptible and sustain curiosity rather than checking exploratory tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach geography to increase spatial/natural perception and history to increase human connections
rubrics_metrics.description: "To 'learn geography' is to gain in power to perceive the spatial, the natural, connections of an ordinary act; to 'learn history' is essentially to gain in power to recognize its human connections."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame geography and history learning as skills that enrich perception of ordinary acts—geography for natural/spatial relations, history for human/social relations—rather than as mere fact memorization.
